newsitem.title: TANZANIA: U.N. Rwanda tribunal set to open amid tight security.
newsitem.headline: U.N. Rwanda tribunal set to open amid tight security.

text.p: The international tribunal on Rwanda's 1994 genocide was set to open in this northern Tanzanian town on Thursday with tight security for the first witnesses to appear in court.

Tribunal officials told Reuters that prosecution witnesses to testify against Jean Paul Akayesu, 43, at the International Criminal Tribunal for Rwanda (ICTR), were being flown in from the Rwandan capital at the last possible moment in an apparent effort to ensure their safety.
Ethiopian chief prosecutor Yacob Haile Mariam was expected to present the witnesses before a three-person panel of judges led by Senegalese judge Laity Kama.
"All we know is that they (witnesses) are en route from Kigali. They are flying and they will be in court," tribunal spokesman Bocar Sy said.
He added: "Absolutely nobody is giving out any information about these witnesses because of tight security."
The tribunal, dogged by delays and allegations of mismanagement, hopes to hear evidence on Akayesu's role in the three-month genocide of an estimated 800,000 Tutsis and moderate Hutus.
The genocide was sparked off by the assassination of Hutu president and military strongman Juvenal Habyarimana in April 1994 as he returned from a regional peace summit in Tanzania.

Angry Hutu mobs, militia and soldiers took up arms and hunted down Tutsis and moderate Hutus opposed to Habyarimana's military junta. The mass slaughter only ended after victorious Tutsi rebels took power and drove the Hutus into exile.
Akayesu, a former mayor in central Rwanda's Taba commune, has pleaded not guilty to charges of crimes against humanity and genocide during the killings between April and June 1994.
His trial was adjourned last October to allow the defence time to prepare its case but will now restart at ICTR headquarters in the northern Tanzanian town of Arusha.
"This is the first time that we will see people who will testify "I saw this or I saw that or I saw someone giving orders to kill'," Sy said by telephone.
The U.N. tribunal had a series of false starts in 1995 with a series of adjournments on procedural grounds.

But far worse for its image was the disclosure last October that U.N. headquarters in New York had sent auditors and investigators to probe the tribunal in Arusha and its prosecution office in Kigali, the Rwandan capital. Details of the inquiry were not made public but were linked to allegations of mismanagement.
The location of the tribunal in Arusha, a town with poor transport connections and telecommunications, has added to delays.
Defence counsel Nicolas Taingaye, a barrister from the Central African Republic, is Akayesu's third lawyer.
Sy said Taingaye was entitled to press the panel of judges for a further postponement.
Jurists had hoped the Arusha trials set up in November 1994 and parallel trials in The Hague for war crimes in the former Yugoslavia would show the world mass killings would not go unpunished.
Genocide trials held by Rwanda under its own genocide law threaten to overshadow the laborious ICTR process.
A Rwandan court convicted and sentenced to death two Hutus this week for genocide and crimes against humanity after a four-hour trial on December 27.
Rwanda has scheduled more trials for next week and the two men, who had no defence lawyers, were given 15 days to appeal.
The maximum sanction available to the U.N. tribunal is life imprisonment.

The ICTR, which had a budget of $36 million in 1996, has indicted 21 suspects of whom 13 are in custody, a tribunal spokeswoman said. Rwanda has around 90,000 Hutus in its jails accused or suspected of crimes related to the genocide.
Trials of seven other suspects have been set between February and August in Arusha.
But analysts say the major players in the genocide are still at large, living comfortably in foreign capitals of Europe, America and Africa.
